prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You have installed a voice that can soothe you: agents of the eaten flesh, every body a cocoon of change— Puparium. The garden a birthing house, sarcophagidae— And green was so dark in the night-garden, in the garden's gourd of air— green's epitome of green's peace, the beautiful inhuman leg-music, crickets' thrum— a pulse to build their houses by, each successive molt a tent of skin in which skin can grow, the metallic sheen of their blue backs as they hatch out, winged and mouthed— Like in a charnel ground, you sit and see. In one of the Eight Great Cemeteries, you sit and see— How the skull-grounds are ringed by flame, how they spread out under a diamond tent, how the adepts pupate among bones— saying I who fear dying, I who fear being dead— Refuge field. See it now. That assembly of sages you would have yourself build, to hear the lineage from mouth to ear, encounter the truth- chain— Saying, Soft eaters, someone's children, who gives them refuge from want— Cynomyopsis Cadavarena. On every tongue they feed.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Puparium, The

outputs.L1:
You have installed a voice that can soothe you: agents of the eaten flesh, every body a cocoon of change—Puparium. The garden, a birthing house; Sarcophagidae. And green was so dark in the night-garden, in the garden’s gourd of air—green, the epitome of green’s own peace; the beautiful, inhuman leg-music, the crickets’ thrum—a pulse by which they build their houses, each successive molt a tent of skin in which skin can grow, the metallic sheen of their blue backs as they hatch out, winged and mouthed.

As in a charnel ground, you sit and see. In one of the Eight Great Cemeteries, you sit and see—how the skull-grounds are ringed by flame, how they spread beneath a diamond tent, how the adepts pupate among bones, saying: I who fear dying, I who fear being dead.

Refuge field. See it now: that assembly of sages you would have yourself build, to hear the lineage passed from mouth to ear, to encounter the truth-chain—saying: Soft eaters, someone’s children, who gives them refuge from want—Cynomyopsis Cadavarena. On every tongue, they feed.
outputs.L2:
You have brought into yourself a calming voice: servants of consumed meat, each organism sealed inside transformation—puparium. The garden becomes a chamber for birth, Sarcophagidae. And in the night garden, inside the gourd-shaped hollow of its air, the green had deepened almost beyond green—green distilled into its own quiet, while the lovely, nonhuman music of legs sounded, the crickets vibrating. Their rhythm was a heartbeat for making dwellings, every molt another skin-shelter where the body could enlarge; their blue backs flashed with metal as they emerged, winged, with mouths.

As if seated in a place of corpses, you remain and look. In one of the Eight Great Cemeteries, you stay there watching: the skull-fields encircled with fire, widening beneath a diamond canopy, the practitioners changing like pupae among bones—speaking: I am the one afraid to die; I am the one afraid of being dead.

A field of refuge. Look at it here. The gathering of wise ones you long to construct for yourself, so the lineage may pass from mouth into ear, so the chain of truth may be met. And you say: gentle devourers, offspring of someone—who shelters them from hunger? Cynomyopsis cadaverina. They feed upon every tongue.
outputs.L3:
The speaker evokes a soothing voice that seems to arise from a place of transformation and decay. This voice is not merely comforting in a gentle or ordinary sense; it is tied to the unsettling processes by which bodies change form, break down, and become something else. Flesh, in this vision, is not fixed or final. It becomes a kind of cocoon, a temporary casing in which change takes place. Decay is therefore presented not only as an ending, but also as a passage into another state of being.

The garden is described as a dark and fertile birthing ground, alive with hidden processes. It is filled with insect life: creatures molt, hatch, feed, and emerge from the soil and shadows. The sounds of crickets create a steady rhythm, suggesting both natural continuity and ritual repetition. This garden is not a peaceful ornamental space, but a living, breathing site of transformation. It is rich with darkness, moisture, and organic change, where life continually rises out of decomposition.

At the same time, the garden is linked to the imagery of a charnel ground or cemetery. It becomes a place where death is fully present: there are flames, bones, remains, and the suggestion of bodies returning to the elements. Yet this space is also spiritual. It is inhabited, or at least imagined, as a place where adepts, sages, or practitioners confront mortality directly. Death and wisdom coexist there. The garden’s darkness is not only terrifying; it is also a place of insight, where the boundary between decay and awakening becomes blurred.

Within this setting, the speaker confronts a deep fear of dying and of being dead. The meditation on bodies, insects, bones, and burial forces the speaker to face mortality without evasion. Yet the speaker also seeks refuge from this fear through a lineage of sages and transmitted truth. Rather than relying only on personal strength, the speaker turns toward inherited wisdom, teachings, and spiritual continuity. The presence of a lineage suggests that refuge is found in truths passed down through generations, truths capable of holding the terror of death within a larger understanding.

The text also emphasizes scavenging creatures, not simply as symbols of decay, but as vulnerable beings in their own right. These creatures feed on flesh, yet they are not portrayed as cruel or monstrous. They too are subject to hunger, need, and suffering. Their scavenging becomes part of the shared condition of life: all beings depend on other beings, and all are exposed to want. In this way, the text extends compassion even to those creatures associated with death and decomposition, recognizing them as living beings who also seek refuge.
outputs.L4:
The body begins in change and ends in change. Even while we name ourselves as fixed beings—this person, this face, this history—life is continually loosening and remaking us. Skin sheds, breath enters and leaves, cells perish and are replaced. Beneath the appearance of continuity, we are already a procession of small disappearances.

In the life of an insect, this truth is visible with startling clarity. A caterpillar does not simply grow wings; it must surrender the shape by which it once knew the world. It enters the chrysalis and becomes, for a time, something almost unrecognizable: a soft dissolution, a body undone from within. What seems like death is also preparation. What seems like decay is also a hidden architecture. From the liquefaction of one form, another form gathers itself.

So too, the human body is not exempt from the law of transformation. In charnel-ground imagery, the corpse is not treated as an obscenity to be hidden from thought, but as a teacher. The body laid open to weather, birds, insects, and time reveals what pride and fear conceal: that flesh belongs to the earth, that beauty is temporary, that identity cannot be preserved by clinging to bone and skin. The charnel ground is terrible because it refuses illusion, but it is also compassionate because it shows the truth without ornament. What we call “my body” is already shared with air, water, microbes, ancestors, and future life.

Decay, then, is not merely an ending. It is a redistribution. The body becomes nourishment. It enters soil, root, wing, and worm. It returns to the dark fertility from which all living things arise. The same matter that once held laughter, hunger, grief, and desire may later feed grass, shelter larvae, or pass into the blood of another creature. Death does not erase participation; it changes its form.

Buddhist refuge practices offer a way to meet this recognition without despair. To take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha is not to escape impermanence, but to turn toward it with steadiness. The Buddha is the awakened one who saw directly into birth, aging, sickness, and death. The Dharma is the teaching that all compounded things are unstable, that suffering arises through attachment, and that liberation begins when we stop demanding permanence from what cannot provide it. The Sangha is the community of beings who practice remembering this together.

In such a refuge, mortality becomes less a punishment than a doorway into wisdom. The fear of dying may still arise; the body still trembles before its own vanishing. But fear is softened by the knowledge that nothing has ever stood apart from change. The self we defend so fiercely is not a sealed chamber, but a temporary gathering. It is made of food, language, memory, weather, love, and the labor of countless beings. When it dissolves, it does not fall out of the world. It returns to the world.

The insect emerging from its chrysalis, the corpse feeding the ground, the practitioner bowing before the mystery of impermanence—all belong to the same teaching. Transformation is not sentimental. It includes rupture, rot, hunger, and loss. Yet it also includes continuity, nourishment, and awakening. The end of one form makes possible the arising of another.

To contemplate death in this way is not to glorify suffering or deny grief. Grief is part of the cycle too, another form of love changing shape. But the meditation asks us to look more deeply than fear allows. It asks us to see that decomposition is not a failure of life, but one of life’s methods. It asks us to understand the grave, the chrysalis, and the altar as places where identity is undone and relation is revealed.

What dies does not remain as it was. Nothing remains as it was. Yet nothing is entirely lost. The world is an immense ceremony of becoming and unbecoming, each body briefly luminous, each ending folded into another beginning. To live with this awareness is to participate more tenderly in existence: to breathe, to feed, to decay, to awaken, and to return.

**The Puparium and You**

The puparium is a small, protective case formed by certain insects during a remarkable stage of transformation. Though it may look simple from the outside, it holds one of nature’s quiet miracles: the process of becoming something new.

You might see a puparium as a symbol of patience and change. Inside, life is not still—it is reorganizing, developing, and preparing for the next stage. The creature within is hidden from view, yet it is moving toward a future form.

The lesson of the puparium is that growth does not always look dramatic. Sometimes, transformation happens in silence. Sometimes, You need time, protection, and patience before emerging stronger than before.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem about fear of death, Tibetan charnel grounds, refuge fields, and flesh-eating flies, using scientific insect terminology and lush garden imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
In the Tibetan charnel ground, where the sky is a blue wound held open by vultures, I kneel among the irises of bone and the marigolds of fat, afraid of the small black door that keeps opening inside my breath. Death is not a skeleton but a garden in accelerated bloom: orchids of cartilage, lilies rooted in marrow, the sweet rot of apples becoming scripture beneath the sun. Around me the flesh-eating flies arrive with priestly precision—Calliphoridae in metallic viridian, Sarcophagidae striped like censers, their aristate antennae trembling over the offerings, their labella tasting salt, their compound eyes jeweled with a thousand tiny apocalypses. They move by instar and appetite, laying ova in the soft sutras of the body; soon larvae, apodous and pale as unspoken mantras, will thresh through the mortal flowerbed, their posterior spiracles breathing at the edge of disappearance.

I look for refuge and find it painted in impossible perspective: a refuge field rising from the carrion meadow, lamas seated on lotus-thrones of peony and smoke, bodhisattvas garlanded with clematis, wrathful deities blazing like poppies after rain. Above them, the lineage tree spreads its branches through the bardo, each leaf a green ear listening to my terror. I want to climb into that painted orchard and hide in the nectar of Tara’s hand, in the saffron pollen of Avalokiteśvara’s gaze; but the flies know there is no hiding. Their halteres tick like tiny ritual drums. Their tarsi bless the torn skin. Their larvae recite the oldest doctrine without words: impermanence is not an idea but a mouth.

The garden grows extravagant. Roses open from empty eye sockets, foxglove bells ring along the ribs, my fear winds itself through the wisteria of nerves. I imagine my own body offered to the high plateau, unbuttoned by beaks, translated by mandibles, softened into weather. How intimate the Diptera are, how devoted to transformation: necrophagous angels with enzymatic prayers, black-winged botanists of the corpse, making of dread a compost rich enough for lotus roots. Still I tremble. Still I cling to the little fence of my name. Yet in the charnel ground, beneath the thunderhead of wings, the refuge field leans closer, lush and terrible, and every fly becomes a seed syllable, every wound a doorway, every decaying petal a teacher whispering: what you love was always made of vanishing; what vanishes feeds the flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental lyric meditation in the second person that begins with “You have installed a voice that can soothe you” and weaves together pupation, sarcophagidae, crickets, cemeteries, and Buddhist imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
You have installed a voice that can soothe you

inside the small dark app of the skull,  
a bell-tone rinsed in rainwater,  
a monk’s thumb circling the bead of your breath.

It says: remain.

So you remain—  
not whole, not broken,  
but pupating in the soft catastrophe  
between names.

Your old body has become a room  
you no longer enter except in dreams.  
There are hooks in the walls.  
There is silk.  
There is the slow furniture of becoming.

Outside, the crickets keep translating the night  
into hunger, hunger, hunger,  
their little black instruments sawing  
at the hem of samsara.

You lie still enough  
to hear the cemeteries thinking.

Stone after stone after stone:  
a congregation of shut mouths,  
each one practicing emptiness  
with greater devotion than you.

Above the grass, Sarcophagidae arrive—  
gray ministers, red-eyed,  
drawn to every doctrine of opening.  
They know the body as scripture,  
know how quickly a temple  
becomes a door.

Do not look away, the voice says,  
and because it is your voice  
wearing the robe of another,  
you obey.

You watch the flies bless what was abandoned.  
You watch the larvae learn the holy syllable  
of flesh.  
You watch the chrysalis darken  
like a thought before compassion.

Somewhere a Buddha sits  
beneath the insect-ridden tree of your ribs,  
not smiling, not judging,  
only touching the earth

as if to say:  
this too is witness.  
This too is the path.  
This too, the grave-wet wing  
unfolding from its sleep.

The crickets continue.

The cemetery continues.

The voice lowers itself into you  
like a lamp into a well:

Breathe in—  
the corpse-flower opens.

Breathe out—  
a bell without a bell.

You are not being saved.  
You are being changed.  
You are the pupa and the shroud,  
the fly and the mantra,  
the stone name softened by moss.

You are learning to be tender  
with the rot that feeds the future.

You are learning  
that even decay  
has a posture of prayer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark ecological poem in a fragmentary, incantatory style about maggots, metamorphosis, the Eight Great Cemeteries, and the desire for spiritual refuge.
counterfactuals.output:
In the wet scripture of the carcass,  
white mouths flower.

Maggots—  
small monks of hunger,  
bead-bodied, blind—  
turn the fallen deer  
into a hymn without music.

O rot, black orchard.  
O breath of the soil  
rising from the split rib.

I have seen the forest kneel  
to its own undoing:  
fungus in the tongue of the log,  
moss drinking the skull’s rain,  
roots braiding through the pelvis  
of what once ran.

Nothing is wasted,  
only renamed.

In the Eight Great Cemeteries,  
where jackals ring the moon  
and bone-fires stutter,  
the saints sit among ash,  
garlanded with endings.

Cool Grove.  
Perfected in Body.  
Lotus Mound.  
Lanka Mound.  
Spontaneously Accomplished.  
Emanated Heap.  
Dense Thicket.  
Secret Grove.

Their names pass through me  
like smoke through a ruined house.

I too am a heap.  
I too am a grove.  
I too carry larvae  
of future wings.

Under the skin,  
a soft revolution:  
matter praying  
by becoming other.

Maggot to fly.  
Leaf to loam.  
Corpse to root.  
Grief to mantra.  
Fear to a door  
I cannot yet open.

O mothers of decay,  
take this panic.  
Take this jeweled self  
I polish and defend.  
Feed it to the bright blind children  
of the earth.

Let them hollow me  
without hatred.

Let them teach me  
the mercy of use,  
the vow of returning,  
the dark green law  
that no body is alone.

In the charnel wind,  
I ask for refuge.

Not in purity.  
Not in escape.  
Not in a sky  
scrubbed clean of vultures.

But here—  
in the compost smoke,  
in the mandala of mandibles,  
in the black rain filling the hoofprint,  
in the fly’s iridescent back  
where a shattered sun  
still trembles.

I bow  
to the cemetery within the seed.

I bow  
to the seed within the wound.

I bow  
to the wound that opens  
and opens  
and opens—

until even the maggot  
is a bell,

until even the corpse  
is a cradle,

until even my terror  
curls inward, softens, splits,

and lifts.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic passage that blends entomology and Vajrayana death meditation: flies hatching from carrion, adepts among bones, fear of dying, and a “refuge field.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the warm scripture of decay, the flies begin their mantra.

From the loosened seam of carrion, white larvae rise—blind commas, milk-pale syllables—turning the body’s last silence into motion. Entomology names them plainly: eggs, instars, pupae, emergence. Yet each stage is a bell struck in the charnel ground. What was feared as ending becomes a swarm of continuities, wings folded inside hunger, flight rehearsed in rot.

Among the bones, the adepts sit without ornament. Ribs arc around them like old moonboats. Skulls hold rainwater and the sky’s reflection. They do not look away from the body as it bloats, darkens, opens; they watch the self’s proud borders soften into feast. Their meditation is not morbid but exact: this flesh was always borrowed, always becoming soil, breath, beak, root, fly.

Still, fear comes.

It comes with a human face—my face—clutching at the throat, whispering, not yet, not me, not this. It trembles before the great subtraction: name from mouth, warmth from hand, beloveds from reach. The adepts let the fear enter and bow. They make of panic a lamp, of the racing heart a drum. They say: Look closely. Even terror is impermanent. Even the one who fears cannot be found.

Above the charnel ground, the refuge field gathers—not elsewhere, not distant, but vivid as blue flame in the mind’s own sky. Lamas, yidams, dakinis, protectors: a mandala of fierce compassion hovering over marrow and wing. Their gazes do not deny the maggots; their blessings do not perfume the corpse. They reveal the inseparability of rot and radiance, the empty brilliance moving through all forms.

Then the flies lift.

Black beads of life rise from the broken vessel, stitching the air with their brief, ecstatic flight. And the adept, seated among bones, breathes into the knowledge that dying is not an error in the world, but one of its deepest teachings: the body given back, the self unfastened, the refuge field opening everywhere—even here, especially here—where fear meets the shining mouth of change.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde prose poem with em dashes and repeated phrases, combining night-garden imagery, insect molts, charnel grounds, lineage transmission, and the phrase “On every tongue they feed.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the night-garden—where the moon bruises the lilies silver, where the soil exhales its black alphabet—we gather the husks of insects like discarded masks, like little saints emptied of their miracles. Again and again, the cicada splits its back and leaves itself behind—again and again, the beetle climbs out of its former name—again and again, the moth becomes a pale rumor on the bark.

Beyond the wall, the charnel ground blooms without flowers. Bones sweeten in the rain. Ash settles on the fennel. The dead do not depart—they root, they whisper, they rise through the stems as bitter sap. Grandmother’s breath in the mint—father’s wound in the thorn—child’s first cry folded into the wings of flies. This is how the lineage passes: not by crown, not by scripture, but by larva, spore, and fever—by the mouth receiving what the mouth cannot keep.

On every tongue they feed. On every tongue they feed.

The ancestors come wearing insect molts—transparent, crackling, almost tender. They teach us how to shed without vanishing. They teach us the old grammar of rot: what falls becomes gate, what opens becomes hunger, what hunger names becomes kin. In the night-garden—under the bitten moon, beside the charnel roses—we taste the dust of those who made us, and the dust tastes back.

On every tongue they feed—on every tongue they bloom—on every tongue the dead lay their small, shining eggs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
